note: Who voices whom. Every voice is an ElevenLabs library voice, found with the voice search (gender, age, descriptives, use case) and chosen from its published description; nobody has listened to them yet. Cast for character, not caricature: no accent performance or vocal stereotype was asked for, and direction tags only shape delivery. Two pairs share a voice because the town's own cast file says they are one person (see 'shared').

elijah.why: Middle-aged American low baritone, measured and unhurried with deliberate pauses and a dry, quiet intensity: a salesman in a suit who never blinks, creepy by being calm rather than by any put-on voice.

smyth.why: Older American male, warm, cheerful and jolly: the overly warm priest. The warmth is the joke; the lines carry the rest.

june.why: Young American woman, calm, cool and collected with a little sass: polite at the counter, curt when pushed.

yang.why: Older male baritone with a plain, natural delivery for an older restaurant owner. No accent was asked for and none is performed: his lines are spoken exactly as written.

twins.why: Dry, flat, quietly exhausted young adult man with minimal pitch movement: arsonists for hire who find the work relaxing. One voice for the pair, as the text gives them one line at a time.

teller.why: Middle-aged American woman, sardonic and flat: the snarky bank teller.

prudence.why: Same voice as the Teller: cast.yaml says the Teller is Prudence Ledbetter.

nurse.why: Older American woman, weathered and raspy: a nurse who has seen everything and teases about it.

gertie.why: Same voice as the Nurse: Nurse Gertie is the Expanded name of the hospital's nurse (the 'prince' of both).

clerk.why: Young American woman, wry and dry, natural and conversational: easy to follow through the tutorial, and the deadpan jokes land without a performance.

grubb.why: Older American male showman, an old-school radio announcer's voice: a mayor who thinks every sentence is a speech.

vane.why: Deep, rough, low middle-aged British male, slow to medium pace: the club owner whose calm is the threat. The only British voice in town, which also sets him apart.

mudge.why: Gritty, grumbling older American man: a bought inspector.

unvoiced.bartender: No line of dialogue: the Pale Horse bartender never speaks in quotes in either pack.
unvoiced.morty: Morty is a skeleton and has no lines.
